difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: one concept (reading a nested select / natural-join / project expression) translated directly into words, about 1 min for a prepared student.
stem:
Consider the following three relations:

$$
\texttt{Car}\ (\texttt{model},\ \texttt{year},\ \underline{\texttt{serial}},\ \texttt{color})
$$

$$
\texttt{Make}\ (\texttt{maker},\ \underline{\texttt{model}})
$$

$$
\texttt{Own}\ (\underline{\texttt{owner}},\ \underline{\texttt{serial}})
$$

A tuple in `Car` represents a specific car of a given `model`, made in a given `year`, with a `serial` number and a `color`. A tuple in `Make` specifies that a `maker` company makes cars of a certain `model`. A tuple in `Own` specifies that an `owner` owns the car with a given `serial` number. Keys are underlined; $(\underline{\texttt{owner}},\ \underline{\texttt{serial}})$ together form key for `Own`. ($\bowtie$ denotes natural join)

$$
\pi_{\texttt{owner}}(\texttt{Own} \bowtie (\sigma_{\texttt{color}=\text{“}\textit{red}\text{”}}(\texttt{Car} \bowtie (\sigma_{\texttt{maker}=\text{“}\textit{ABC}\text{”}}\texttt{Make}))))
$$

Which one of the following options describes what the above expression computes?

options.label: A
options.text: All owners of a red car, a car made by ABC, or a red car made by ABC

options.label: B
options.text: All owners of more than one car, where at least one car is red and made by ABC

options.label: C
options.text: All owners of a red car made by ABC

options.label: D
options.text: All red cars made by ABC

solution.quick: Read the expression from the inside out. $\sigma_{\texttt{maker}=\text{“ABC”}}\texttt{Make}$ keeps the models made by ABC. Joining with `Car` on `model` keeps only cars of those models, and $\sigma_{\texttt{color}=\text{“red”}}$ keeps the red ones: these are the **red cars made by ABC**. Joining with `Own` on `serial` attaches their owners, and $\pi_{\texttt{owner}}$ outputs only the owners. So the expression computes all owners of a red car made by ABC. Answer **(C)**.

steps.title: Find the join attributes
steps.body:
A natural join $R \bowtie S$ matches tuples on **all attributes with the same name** and keeps one copy of each.

- $\texttt{Car}(\texttt{model}, \texttt{year}, \texttt{serial}, \texttt{color})$ and $\texttt{Make}(\texttt{maker}, \texttt{model})$ share only `model`. So $\texttt{Car} \bowtie (\dots\texttt{Make})$ pairs each car with the maker of its model.
- That result has the attributes $(\texttt{model}, \texttt{year}, \texttt{serial}, \texttt{color}, \texttt{maker})$. It shares only `serial` with $\texttt{Own}(\texttt{owner}, \texttt{serial})$, so $\texttt{Own} \bowtie (\dots)$ pairs each car with the people who own it.

steps.title: Innermost: models made by ABC
steps.body:
$$\sigma_{\texttt{maker}=\text{“ABC”}}(\texttt{Make})$$

keeps only the `Make` tuples whose maker is ABC. The result is the set of models that ABC makes, each written as a tuple $(\text{ABC}, \texttt{model})$.

steps.title: Middle: red cars made by ABC
steps.body:
$\texttt{Car} \bowtie \sigma_{\texttt{maker}=\text{“ABC”}}(\texttt{Make})$ keeps a car only if its `model` appears among ABC's models, so it lists exactly the cars made by ABC (with `maker` = ABC attached).

Then $\sigma_{\texttt{color}=\text{“red”}}(\cdot)$ keeps only the red ones. A tuple survives only if it passed **both** filters, so the two conditions are combined with AND:

$$\sigma_{\texttt{color}=\text{“red”}}\big(\texttt{Car} \bowtie \sigma_{\texttt{maker}=\text{“ABC”}}(\texttt{Make})\big) = \text{cars that are red } \textbf{and } \text{made by ABC}.$$

steps.title: Outer: attach owners, keep only the owner column
steps.body:
$\texttt{Own} \bowtie (\dots)$ matches each red ABC car with every `Own` tuple that has the same `serial`. The result has one row per (owner, red ABC car) pair. An owner with no red ABC car contributes no row.

$\pi_{\texttt{owner}}$ keeps only the `owner` column and removes duplicates (relational algebra has set semantics). An owner of two red ABC cars therefore appears once.

**Result:** the set of all owners who own at least one red car made by ABC.

steps.title: Check on a small instance
steps.body:
Let `Make` = {(ABC, m1), (XYZ, m2), (ABC, m3)} and

| `model` | `year` | `serial` | `color` | maker (via `Make`) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| m1 | 2020 | 1 | red | ABC |
| m2 | 2021 | 2 | red | XYZ |
| m1 | 2022 | 3 | blue | ABC |
| m3 | 2019 | 4 | red | ABC |
| m2 | 2018 | 5 | blue | XYZ |

with `Own` = {(P, 1), (Q, 2), (R, 3), (S, 4), (S, 5), (T, 5)}.

- ABC models: m1, m3. Cars made by ABC: serials 1, 3, 4. Red among them: serials **1, 4**.
- Owners of serials 1 and 4: **P** and **S**. The expression returns $\{P, S\}$.

Compare with the options on this instance:

- (A) owners of a red car *or* an ABC car: $\{P, Q, R, S\}$. This is different, because Q (red XYZ car) and R (blue ABC car) are included.
- (B) owners of more than one car with at least one red ABC car: $\{S\}$. This is different, because P owns only one car.
- (C) owners of a red ABC car: $\{P, S\}$. This **matches**.
- (D) red ABC cars: serials $\{1, 4\}$. These are cars, not owners.

The answer is **(C)**.

solution.teaching:
**The three operators used here.**

- **Selection** $\sigma_{\text{condition}}(R)$ keeps the *rows* of $R$ that satisfy the condition. The columns are unchanged.
- **Projection** $\pi_{A_1,\dots,A_k}(R)$ keeps only the listed *columns*. Because a relation is a set, duplicate rows are removed.
- **Natural join** $R \bowtie S$ pairs every tuple of $R$ with every tuple of $S$ that agrees on **all common attribute names**, and keeps one copy of those common attributes. A row of $R$ with no partner in $S$ disappears.

**How to read a nested expression.** Work from the innermost parentheses outward and translate each operator into words. $\sigma$ means "keep those that…", $\bowtie$ means "link to the matching rows of…", and $\pi$ means "report only…". The join attributes come from the schemas. Here `model` links `Car` to `Make`, and `serial` links `Own` to `Car`.

**Why stacked filters mean AND.** A selection applied to the output of another selection (or of a join that already filtered rows) can only remove more rows. So $\sigma_{c_2}(\sigma_{c_1}(R)) = \sigma_{c_1 \wedge c_2}(R)$. Joining with a *filtered* `Make` works as a filter on `Car` too: a car survives only if its model is an ABC model. An OR ("red **or** ABC") would need a union of two separate results, $\sigma_{\text{red}}(\dots) \cup \sigma_{\text{ABC}}(\dots)$, or a disjunctive condition. Nothing like that appears here.

**What the join with `Own` does.** A natural join is an existence test plus attachment. An owner appears in the result if **at least one** of their cars matches, and owning one such car is enough. Counting ("more than one car") would need an aggregation, or a self-join of `Own` with an inequality on `serial`. This expression has neither.

**Back to the question.** Inside out: models by ABC, then cars of those models, then the red ones, then who owns them, then only the names. That is "all owners of a red car made by ABC", option (C).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: The two filters are applied one after the other, so a car must be red **and** made by ABC. The expression never takes a union, so owners of a red non-ABC car, or of a non-red ABC car, are not returned. In the instance above, option (A) would wrongly include Q and R.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Nothing in the expression counts cars. The natural join with `Own` keeps an owner as soon as **one** of their cars is a red ABC car, so an owner of exactly one such car (P in the instance) is in the result. Option (B) would wrongly exclude P.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: $\sigma_{\text{red}}(\texttt{Car} \bowtie \sigma_{\text{ABC}}\texttt{Make})$ gives the red ABC cars. The join with `Own` on `serial` attaches their owners, and $\pi_{\texttt{owner}}$ returns the distinct owners. This is exactly "all owners of a red car made by ABC".

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: This describes only the inner subexpression $\sigma_{\text{red}}(\texttt{Car} \bowtie \sigma_{\text{ABC}}\texttt{Make})$. The outer join with `Own` and the projection $\pi_{\texttt{owner}}$ turn it into a list of **owners**, not cars.

solution.shortcut: Read inside out and turn each operator into words: $\sigma$ = "which are", $\bowtie$ = "linked to", $\pi$ = "report only". Stacked selections are ANDed, and the outermost $\pi$ tells you what kind of object is returned (here, owners).
solution.commonTrap: Treating the two selections as an OR and choosing (A). Selections applied in sequence (with a join in between) combine with **AND**, so a car must be both red and made by ABC. The other trap is stopping at the inner subexpression and choosing (D), which ignores the join with `Own` and the final $\pi_{\texttt{owner}}$.

Relation/attribute names in typewriter font are rendered as \texttt / inline code; the paper wording "together form key for Own" (without "the") is kept as printed.

answerVerification.independentAnswer: C (all owners of a red car made by ABC)
answerVerification.checkCode:
# Relations as lists of dicts; natural join / select / project on sets of tuples
def nat_join(R, S):
    common = set(R[0]) & set(S[0]) if R and S else set()
    return [{**r, **s} for r in R for s in S if all(r[a] == s[a] for a in common)]
sel = lambda R, p: [t for t in R if p(t)]
proj = lambda R, a: {t[a] for t in R}
Car = [dict(model='m1', year=2020, serial=1, color='red'),   # ABC, red
       dict(model='m2', year=2021, serial=2, color='red'),   # XYZ, red
       dict(model='m1', year=2022, serial=3, color='blue'),  # ABC, blue
       dict(model='m3', year=2019, serial=4, color='red'),   # ABC, red
       dict(model='m2', year=2018, serial=5, color='blue')]  # XYZ, blue
Make = [dict(maker='ABC', model='m1'), dict(maker='XYZ', model='m2'), dict(maker='ABC', model='m3')]
Own = [dict(owner='P', serial=1),                              # P: one red ABC car
       dict(owner='Q', serial=2),                              # Q: red, not ABC
       dict(owner='R', serial=3),                              # R: ABC, not red
       dict(owner='S', serial=4), dict(owner='S', serial=5),   # S: red ABC + another car
       dict(owner='T', serial=5)]                              # T: blue XYZ only
inner = sel(nat_join(Car, sel(Make, lambda t: t['maker'] == 'ABC')), lambda t: t['color'] == 'red')
expr = proj(nat_join(Own, inner), 'owner')
print('red ABC cars (serials):', sorted(t['serial'] for t in inner))
print('expression result     :', sorted(expr))
maker = {m['model']: m['maker'] for m in Make}
car = {c['serial']: c for c in Car}
owns = {}
for o in Own: owns.setdefault(o['owner'], []).append(car[o['serial']])
red = lambda c: c['color'] == 'red'; abc = lambda c: maker[c['model']] == 'ABC'
A = {o for o, cs in owns.items() if any(red(c) or abc(c) for c in cs)}
B = {o for o, cs in owns.items() if len(cs) > 1 and any(red(c) and abc(c) for c in cs)}
C = {o for o, cs in owns.items() if any(red(c) and abc(c) for c in cs)}
print('A:', sorted(A), A == expr); print('B:', sorted(B), B == expr); print('C:', sorted(C), C == expr)
print('D is a set of cars (serials), not owners:', sorted(t['serial'] for t in inner))
answerVerification.notes: Blind re-solve (done before reading the key or the stored solution): sigma_{maker=ABC}(Make) gives ABC models; joining with Car on model (Make key is model, so each model has one maker) gives cars made by ABC; sigma_{color=red} keeps the red ones (AND of both filters); joining with Own on serial attaches owners; pi_owner returns distinct owners. Result = owners of at least one red ABC car = option (C), matching official key C. The Python check evaluates the expression on a small instance and compares with each option: expression {P, S}; A {P, Q, R, S}; B {S}; C {P, S}; D is a set of cars, not owners.
